title: Sweden’s Government Offices block ChatGPT and Claude and keep Copilot, Pennsylvania requires labels on misleading AI ads, and Kimi K3.1 Pro nearly matches Claude Opus 5.5 on coding. Elvis’s rights holders sue Anthropic, Meta delays its crawling terms, Google lets AI Mode data shape ads, Claude Enterprise adds spend controls, Claude Code gets MCP Tasks, Dayforce buys an AI interviewer, and AWS is sold out through 2027.
summary: On 22 and 23 October 2026: Sweden’s Government Offices said they will block ChatGPT and Claude on staff computers from 26 October, keeping only Microsoft Copilot. Pennsylvania’s governor signed a law requiring labels on ads that use AI content in a misleading way. Moonshot released Kimi K3.1 Pro, with open weights due by 4 November. Elvis Presley’s rights holders sued Anthropic over 274 songs. Meta pushed its website-crawling business terms to 20 November. Google’s privacy policy now lets Gmail and Photos data shared with AI Mode inform ads. Anthropic unified chat and Cowork in Claude Enterprise with new spend controls, and brought MCP Tasks and Elicitations to Claude Code. Dayforce agreed to buy Ribbon AI. Amazon’s CEO said AWS capacity is largely sold out through 2027.
uncertainty: Sweden’s block comes from Swedish Radio’s reporting via Decrypt; the Government Offices have not said whether their Copilot setup includes Claude models. The Verge says Pennsylvania’s law covers text ads, but the bill text exempts content ‘limited to text’; we follow the bill text. The Elvis claims are allegations that no court has ruled on. Kimi’s benchmark figures are Moonshot’s own and have not been checked independently. Google says ads will not be based ‘directly’ on Gmail or Photos. Upstash’s details on Claude Code versions and surfaces are its own reading of Anthropic’s release. Jassy’s comments come from a podcast reported by Reuters.

stories.theme: Sweden’s Government Offices block ChatGPT and Claude on staff computers and keep only Copilot
stories.changed: On Friday 23 October 2026 Swedish Radio reported that Sweden’s Government Offices, which support the prime minister and cabinet, will block ChatGPT and Claude on staff computers from Monday 26 October, leaving Microsoft Copilot as the only approved AI tool. In a post on the staff intranet, digitalisation director Mikael Wettercrantz said using AI services without a formal contract can have ‘consequences for our information security’, and that there had been several examples of problematic use, both in the sensitivity of what was typed in and in how the answers were handled. Copilot is allowed because the Government Offices reviewed it and raised its security settings afterwards. Some staff can still reach the blocked tools through an AI platform built internally. Sweden’s Tax Agency and National Board of Institutional Care already block similar tools, and the Enforcement Authority is preparing its own decision.
stories.matters: A government is drawing the line between AI tools it has a contract and security review for, and consumer AI services it does not. Many employers are heading the same way.
stories.imply: Staff using personal AI accounts for work are the risk employers are now acting on. Expect more ‘approved tools only’ rules, with a sanctioned alternative.
uses: List which AI tools staff actually use for work, including personal accounts.
Decide which tools have a contract and security review, and say so in one short policy.
Offer an approved alternative before you block anything, so work does not move to phones.
stories.example: A city council finds staff pasting case notes into a free chatbot. It blocks the site on work laptops, turns on its enterprise assistant with stricter settings, and runs a 20-minute briefing.
stories.audience: IT and security leaders, public sector managers, and anyone writing an AI use policy.
stories.watch: Whether more Swedish agencies follow. How many staff keep access through the internal platform. Whether the Copilot setup includes Claude models, which are off by default in the EU.

source.title: Decrypt: Sweden's Government Offices Block ChatGPT and Claude, Keep Microsoft Copilot, 24 October 2026
source.quote: We have seen several examples of problematic use of open AI services.

stories.theme: Pennsylvania now requires a label on ads that use AI-made content in a misleading way
stories.changed: On Thursday 22 October 2026 Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act (Senate Bill 806). Advertisers may not knowingly, recklessly or willfully run an ad that uses synthetic content, meaning images, video, audio or text significantly modified or generated by AI, in a way that creates a false impression about the nature, origin or authenticity of the goods or services, without a clear and conspicuous disclosure. The label must say the ad contains content modified or generated using AI, appear the first time the content is shown, be in the same medium as the ad and, where technically feasible, be permanent or very hard to remove. The bill text exempts content that is evidently fictional, parody, satire, commentary or criticism, or limited to text. The Attorney General or a district attorney can seek an injunction, and courts can award a civil fine of up to $3,000 plus fees. The law takes effect in 60 days.
stories.matters: Marketing teams now need a rule for when AI-made images, voices or video in an ad need a label. The Verge notes it applies wherever an ad was made, if it runs in Pennsylvania.
stories.imply: AI disclosure is moving from platform policy into state law. National campaigns will need one labelling approach that works in the strictest state.
uses: Ask marketing to flag every live ad that uses AI-generated people, voices or product shots.
Agree a standard label wording and placement for each format: video, audio and still image.
Ask agencies to confirm in writing whether AI was used in the work they deliver.
stories.example: A retailer’s holiday spot uses an AI-generated shopper holding its blender. Legal adds an on-screen ‘contains AI-generated content’ label from the first frame for the Pennsylvania buy.
stories.audience: Marketing, brand and legal teams, ad agencies and media buyers.
stories.watch: The effective date about 60 days after signing. How ‘significantly modified’ and ‘false consumer perception’ are read. Similar bills in other states.

source.title: The Verge: Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads, 24 October 2026
source.quote: Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content.

stories.theme: Elvis Presley’s rights holders sue Anthropic over training on 274 songs
stories.changed: On Friday 23 October 2026 Authentic Brands Group, the licensing group that controls Elvis Presley’s music and likeness, sued Anthropic, the company behind Claude, Rolling Stone reports. The case, ABE EPE LLC v. Anthropic, says Anthropic trained its models on 274 Presley songs without permission, from ‘All Shook Up’ and ‘Can’t Help Falling in Love’ to lesser-known tracks, and seeks $150,000 per infringed song, roughly $41 million. It alleges Claude produces infringing output of songs and, after guardrails were added, still recreated songs ‘for a modern audience’ with the same structure and hooks. Lead attorney Richard Busch argued the ‘Blurred Lines’ case for Marvin Gaye’s estate. Rolling Stone calls it one of the first major cases brought by an artist’s estate rather than labels or the RIAA. These are allegations; Anthropic has not been found liable.
stories.matters: Rights holders are now suing over specific catalogues, song by song. Content your teams generate with AI that echoes well-known works carries legal risk.
stories.imply: Expect more estates and catalogue owners to sue AI companies. Rewriting a famous song with AI is not a safe way around copyright.
uses: Tell marketing and video teams not to ask AI tools to recreate or ‘modernise’ known songs or lyrics.
Use licensed or properly cleared music for ads and social content, even if AI helped make the rest.
Ask your AI vendors what indemnity they offer for copyright claims over outputs.
stories.example: A social team wants a jingle ‘in the style of’ a 1950s hit. It commissions an original track instead and keeps the licence on file.
stories.audience: Marketing, creative, legal and music teams, and anyone using AI for audio or lyrics.
stories.watch: Anthropic’s response. Whether other estates file similar suits. How the court treats training versus output claims.

source.title: Rolling Stone: Elvis Presley Rightsholders Sue Anthropic for Training on 274 Songs Without Permission, 24 October 2026
source.quote: The Elvis Plaintiffs are deeply protective of these iconic songs,

stories.theme: Meta delays new business terms that let it crawl linked websites, but keeps the wording
stories.changed: On Friday 23 October 2026 Reuters reported that Meta has moved the start of its new business terms from 30 October to 20 November. The terms apply to businesses that use Meta’s tools, such as ads, Facebook Pages or Instagram business accounts, and let Meta send automated crawlers to websites linked to those accounts and use the content to develop its advertising and business products; businesses accept them just by using the tools. Meta said the delay is to explain ‘what’s changing and what’s not’, but the wording looked the same. It removed the word ‘train’ from the terms last week after an outcry, and says site owners can still use robots.txt. The News/Media Alliance, representing more than 2,000 US publishers, had demanded the terms be withdrawn, saying publishers cannot really block Meta’s crawlers because their ads need them. European publishers asked regulators in the EU and UK to suspend the terms, and Britain’s competition watchdog asked Meta to explain them.
stories.matters: Any company with a Facebook Page or Meta ads account may be agreeing to let Meta crawl its website. That can include content you would not want used for Meta’s AI or ad products.
stories.imply: Using an ad platform can now mean handing over website content. Check platform terms as carefully as you check AI vendor terms.
uses: Ask marketing which websites are linked to your Meta business accounts.
Have legal read the new terms before 20 November and decide whether to object or change settings.
Review your robots.txt rules for Meta’s crawlers, knowing ads may still need access.
stories.example: A publisher’s legal team maps which of its sites are tied to its Meta ad accounts and sends the CMA its concerns before the 20 November start.
stories.audience: Marketing and legal teams, publishers, and any business advertising on Facebook or Instagram.
stories.watch: Whether Meta changes the wording before 20 November. Responses from UK and EU regulators. The publishers’ lawsuits against Meta.

source.title: The Next Web: Meta delays its website-crawling terms after a publisher backlash, 23 October 2026
source.quote: to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not

stories.theme: Google’s privacy policy now lets Gmail and Photos data shared with AI Mode shape ads
stories.changed: On Friday 23 October 2026 Ars Technica and The Verge reported a change Google made to its privacy policy on 16 October. The policy used to say Google does not show personalised ads based on content from Drive, Gmail or Photos; it now adds ‘unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads’. That covers people who connect those apps to Search tools such as AI Mode through Google’s Personal Intelligence feature, where sponsored content can appear. Google told Ars that connecting apps is entirely opt-in, that ads will not be based directly on a Gmail inbox or Photos library, and that sensitive information will not be used to tailor ads. Ars says Personal Intelligence can be switched off in Gemini settings or under Data & privacy in a Google account.
stories.matters: Staff who connect a personal Gmail or Drive to Google’s AI search may be feeding what they share there into ad targeting. Work content kept in personal accounts goes with it.
stories.imply: Connecting your apps to an AI assistant can widen how your data is used. Treat ‘connect your apps’ prompts as a privacy decision, not a convenience.
uses: Remind staff not to keep work files in personal Gmail or Drive accounts.
Check whether Personal Intelligence is on in your own Google account, and turn it off if you do not want this.
Add AI ‘connected apps’ settings to your privacy and acceptable-use guidance.
stories.example: A consultant who forwards client drafts to her personal Gmail switches off Personal Intelligence and moves the files into the firm’s managed Drive.
stories.audience: Privacy and IT teams, HR, and anyone who uses personal Google accounts near work data.
stories.watch: Whether regulators question the change. How it applies to Workspace accounts. Ads appearing in more AI search surfaces.

source.title: Ars Technica: Updated Google privacy policy says your Gmail might be used for advertising, 23 October 2026
source.quote: Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or Photos library, and as always, sensitive information will not be used to tailor ads.

stories.theme: Claude Enterprise merges chat and Cowork, with new controls to cap what agentic work costs
stories.changed: On Friday 23 October 2026 Anthropic made its unified Claude experience generally available on Claude Enterprise plans: chat and Cowork are now one Claude on web, desktop and mobile. A conversation starts as a chat; when a task needs code or files, Claude continues in a cloud session, each in its own isolated virtual machine with network egress off by default and connector credentials kept outside the sandbox, and the work keeps going after someone closes their laptop. Pricing stays usage-based, and Anthropic notes agentic work can use more tokens than a quick chat. Admins get four controls: a new Efficient mode that keeps the experience on Sonnet and Haiku models, model entitlements by role, spend limits at organisation, group and member level, and pooled monthly group budgets. Admins manage the rollout in Organization settings; organisations using zero data retention for Claude Code, a HIPAA-ready setup or customer-managed keys stay on their current configuration.
stories.matters: When every chat can turn into an agent job, AI spend can jump without anyone choosing a bigger tool. These controls let finance and IT set limits before it does.
stories.imply: AI budgets are moving to per-role and per-team controls, like cloud spend. Someone needs to own them.
uses: Turn on Efficient mode for teams whose work does not need the largest models.
Set spend limits per group and a pooled budget for heavy users, then review monthly.
Check whether your organisation is on a ZDR, HIPAA or customer-key setup that stays on the old configuration.
stories.example: A 400-person firm puts support and sales on Efficient mode, gives analysts Opus access with a pooled monthly budget, and reviews usage after the first month.
stories.audience: IT admins, finance and procurement teams, and managers of teams using Claude.
stories.watch: Usage bills after rollout. When ZDR and HIPAA customers can move. Similar spend controls from OpenAI and Microsoft.

source.title: Claude by Anthropic: Claude Cowork and chat come together for Enterprise, 23 October 2026
source.quote: Efficient mode is a new setting that keeps the unified Claude experience on Sonnet and Haiku models.

stories.theme: Claude Code can now hand slow jobs to tools and get asked questions mid-task
stories.changed: On Friday 23 October 2026 Anthropic’s ClaudeDevs account said MCP Tasks and Elicitations are available in the Claude Code CLI and rolling out to more Claude products soon, a day after MCP co-creator David Soria Parra announced Tasks support at AGNTCon + MCPCon in San Jose. With Tasks, part of the 2026-07-28 MCP release, a slow tool such as a deep research job answers at once with a task ID; Claude Code keeps working, checks on the task and uses the result when it is done. Elicitations let a tool pause and ask the user a question, such as ‘Deploy to staging?’, shown as a small form in the terminal. Upstash, which published a toolkit for adding Tasks to MCP servers, says Tasks is a public beta from Claude Code v2.1.304, in interactive terminal sessions, the Agent SDK and GitHub Actions, but not yet in the VS Code extension or desktop app, and questions are only shown in interactive terminal sessions.
stories.matters: Agents no longer have to sit and wait on long jobs, or guess when they should check with a person. Both make agent workflows faster and safer.
stories.imply: Long-running agent work with human check-ins is becoming standard in the protocol, not a custom add-on. Tool builders should design for it.
uses: Teams building MCP servers: return a task ID for slow jobs like reports, exports or test runs.
Add an elicitation before risky steps such as deploys, deletes or payments.
Update Claude Code to v2.1.304 or later before testing.
stories.example: A platform team’s deploy tool now asks ‘Deploy to staging?’ inside Claude Code before it runs, and its nightly report tool returns a task ID instead of timing out.
stories.audience: Developers and platform teams building MCP servers or using Claude Code.
stories.watch: Support in the VS Code extension and desktop app. Other MCP clients adding Tasks. Admin controls over what elicitations can ask.

source.title: Upstash Blog: MCP Tasks and Elicitations in Claude Code: Long-Running Tools That Can Ask You Things, 23 October 2026
source.quote: Elicitations allow tools to pause execution until the user responds, even from inside a task.

stories.theme: Moonshot’s Kimi K3.1 Pro nearly matches Claude Opus 5.5 on coding, with open weights by 4 November
stories.changed: On Friday 23 October 2026 Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro, a more heavily post-trained version of its open-weight Kimi K3, with a 1-million-token context window, 2.8 trillion total and 104 billion active parameters, and multimodal input. It is live in the Kimi apps, Kimi Work, Kimi Code and the Kimi API, alongside a Highspeed version Moonshot says runs two to three times faster; full weights are due by 4 November. Moonshot reports 65.7% on the Terminal-Bench 4.0 coding test, ahead of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra at 58.2% and just behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 66.4%, and says false claims on its own stress test fell to 8.3% from 23.4%. It says it removed hacking-related training data before the open release: on its exploit test the released model solved 81% against 90.5% without the cuts. Kimi Enterprise admins must switch it on; API customers can get zero data retention.
stories.matters: A model you can download and run on your own servers is now close to the best closed models on coding work, by its maker’s numbers.
stories.imply: Open-weight models are a real option for sensitive or high-volume work. The decision is now about hosting, security and support, not just capability.
uses: Test it against your current model on a few real coding or finance tasks before 4 November.
Ask security whether a self-hosted open model would let you keep code and data in-house.
Check the licence and the hosting cost once the weights are published.
stories.example: A bank’s engineering team runs K3.1 Pro and its current model side by side on 30 internal bug fixes and compares results and token costs.
stories.audience: Engineering leaders, AI platform teams and security teams evaluating models.
stories.watch: The weights release by 4 November and its licence. Independent benchmark results. US and EU rules on Chinese models.

source.title: The Next Web: Moonshot releases Kimi K3.1 Pro and says it cut its hacking skills, 23 October 2026
source.quote: The figures are Moonshot’s own and have not been checked independently.

stories.theme: Dayforce is buying Ribbon, whose AI interviews job candidates by voice and video
stories.changed: On Friday 23 October 2026 HR software company Dayforce said it has agreed to acquire Ribbon AI, a recruiting technology company. Ribbon’s voice AI interviewer runs two-way interviews around the clock; starting from a job description, it can generate interview questions and a scoring rubric from relevant past interviews, and evaluates candidates from the interview transcripts. Built-in integrity checks look for unusual audio, gaze and response-timing patterns. Dayforce says Ribbon has hundreds of customers and more than one million completed interviews, also offers AI sourcing and outreach by SMS, WhatsApp and email, and is close to finishing an AI scheduling agent. After the deal closes, Ribbon will be built into a new Dayforce Agentic Recruiting experience. The price was not disclosed.
stories.matters: AI interviews are moving from niche tools into the HR platforms big employers already use. More candidates will meet an AI before they meet a recruiter.
stories.imply: Screening decisions will increasingly rest on AI-written rubrics and transcripts. Employers need to be able to explain and check them.
uses: HR teams: ask which hiring steps in your HR software already use AI scoring.
Have a person review AI interview scores before any candidate is rejected.
Tell candidates clearly when an AI is interviewing them and how it is used.
stories.example: A retailer hiring 500 seasonal staff uses AI interviews for first screens, but a recruiter reviews every rejection and samples ten scored interviews a week.
stories.audience: HR and talent teams, hiring managers, and legal teams advising on hiring.
stories.watch: When the deal closes. How Dayforce handles bias audits and candidate consent. Local rules on AI in hiring.

source.title: Dayforce: Dayforce to acquire Ribbon AI Inc. to advance agentic recruiting, 23 October 2026
source.quote: High-volume hiring shouldn’t mean choosing between speed and a strong candidate experience,

stories.theme: Amazon’s CEO says AWS capacity is largely sold out through 2027
stories.changed: On Friday 23 October 2026 Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on a video podcast with Andreessen Horowitz’s Ben Horowitz and Erik Torenberg that AWS cloud capacity is largely sold out through 2027, with significant commitments into 2028, as AI labs and businesses buy up infrastructure, Reuters reports. He said capacity for 2026 is already sold out and that Amazon ‘could invest a lot more and it wouldn’t be a bad use of capital’. Amazon has said it will spend about $220 billion on capital expenditure in 2026. Jassy said AWS always keeps some capacity for on-demand use and for its Bedrock and EC2 services, but has sold ‘all the big chunks’.
stories.matters: If the biggest cloud is booked for years, companies planning large AI projects may face waits, higher prices or less choice of region and hardware.
stories.imply: Computing power for AI is a scarce resource to plan for, like any other supply contract. Big AI plans need capacity commitments early.
uses: Ask IT whether any 2027 AI projects depend on capacity you have not reserved.
Talk to your cloud account manager now about commitments for heavy AI workloads.
Keep a second provider or a smaller model option in your plans.
stories.example: A logistics firm planning to run its own forecasting models in 2027 asks AWS and a second cloud for capacity quotes this quarter, instead of next year.
stories.audience: CIOs, cloud and finance teams, and leaders planning large AI projects.
stories.watch: Amazon’s results on 29 October. Price changes for reserved AI capacity. Similar comments from Microsoft and Google.

source.title: CNA (Reuters): Amazon cloud capacity sold out through 2027, CEO Jassy says, 23 October 2026
